meta.title: Who really said "You cannot teach a man anything; you can only help him to find it within himself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Galileo. The wording is Edgar Quinet’s, from an 1845 polemic against the Roman Church — his summary of Galileo’s method, not a quotation of him.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You cannot teach a man anything; you can only help him to find it within himself'?
meta.ogDescription: It is in none of Galileo’s works. The earliest printing we found is Quinet 1845, p. 62 — unquoted, unsourced, beside the phrase “this Socrates of the modern world.”

answer.label: Not Galileo — Edgar Quinet, summarising him in 1845
answer.authorDates: 1803–1875 · French historian, poet and politician; professor at the Collège de France
answer.sourceLine: Galileo wrote nothing of the kind, and Wikiquote does not list it among his sourced, attributed or misattributed quotations ↗ — it appears on that page only as the caption under his portrait, with no citation. The earliest printing we could find and read is Edgar Quinet’s Ultramontanism; or, The Roman Church and Modern Society (New York: Gates & Stedman, 1845), p. 62 ↗: “His fundamental maxim, that one cannot teach another person the truth, that one can only help him to find it in himself, which is the foundation of his method, is in itself a whole philosophy.” That is Quinet’s sentence about Galileo, in Quinet’s words, without quotation marks and without a source — written 203 years after Galileo died, in a book attacking the Church that tried him.

source.heading: A maxim ascribed, not quoted

docMeta.dd: Ultramontanism; or, The Roman Church and Modern Society
Edgar Quinet (1803–1875), of the Collège de France
New York: Gates & Stedman, 114 William Street, 1845; edited by C. Edwards Lester, translator unnamed
Quinet’s own prose — no quotation marks, no footnote, no source

source.excerpt: I would that some one might undertake to seek out in the confidences which escaped here and there from this great man, in some hidden and brilliant fragments, what was the secret demon of this Socrates of the modern world. For think not that chance alone conducts him in his discoveries. His fundamental maxim, that one cannot teach another person the truth, that one can only help him to find it in himself, which is the foundation of his method, is in itself a whole philosophy; it would suffice to place an abyss between him and the purely sensualist schools.
trail: English Wikiquote’s Galileo page ↗ carries the sentence as a photo caption and nowhere else: it is not in the sourced quotations from the Dialogue, Il Saggiatore or the letters, not under “Attributed,” and not under “Misattributed.” Nothing on that page gives it a source.

A contributor to Wikiquote’s talk page for Galileo ↗ posted a trace back to E. Quinet, The Roman Church and Modern Society, ed. and trans. C. Edwards Lester (New York, 1845), p. 62, giving the wording as “One cannot teach another person the truth, … one can only help him to find it in himself.” A talk page is not a source, so we went and read the book.

Page 62 of the 1845 scan ↗ has it exactly there, in Quinet’s own sentence, with no quotation marks and no citation attached — and with Galileo described three lines above as “this Socrates of the modern world.”

Quinet held a chair at the Collège de France from 1842 ↗ and, with Michelet, used it for a running polemic against the Jesuits and Ultramontanism; Wikipedia notes that books bearing exactly those two titles appeared in 1843 and 1844. This 1845 New York volume is the English of the second. We could not obtain the French original, so we cannot say what Quinet’s own words for the maxim were — only that the English sentence in circulation is this translator’s.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1845 scan. The two sentences above are consecutive paragraphs on the page, run together here. Two things about them are worth noticing. The first is grammatical: his fundamental maxim, that… is a reported proposition, not a reported sentence — Quinet is saying what Galileo believed, and choosing his own English words for it. The second is what stands two sentences earlier: Quinet has just called Galileo “this Socrates of the modern world.” The maxim he then hands him is the Socratic one.

sourceLink.text: Quinet, Ultramontanism (1845), p. 62, at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: Quinet’s book was published in New York in 1845 ↗ and is long out of copyright, as is the anonymous translation printed in it. The sentence at the top of this page is a different matter, and the difference is not only cosmetic: Quinet’s line says one cannot teach another person the truth, where the circulating version says a man cannot be taught anything. Who made that change, and when, we could not establish — so we assert no rights status for the wording as quoted rather than guess one.

author.name: Edgar Quinet
author.heading: About Edgar Quinet
author.bio: Edgar Jean Louis Quinet was born in 1803 and made his name translating and arguing with German philosophy before taking a chair in Paris in 1842. He used it, with his friend Jules Michelet, for a sustained public attack on the Jesuits and on papal authority — the lectures behind Des Jésuites (1843) and L’Ultramontanisme (1844), the second of which reached New York in English in 1845 carrying the sentence on this page. He was driven out of France after Napoleon III’s coup, spent the Second Empire in exile, returned after Sedan, and was elected a deputy to the National Assembly. He died in 1875.

The wording comes from Edgar Quinet, Ultramontanism; or, The Roman Church and Modern Society, ed. C. Edwards Lester (New York: Gates & Stedman, 1845), p. 62, where Quinet writes in his own prose, unquoted and unsourced, that Galileo's "fundamental maxim" was "that one cannot teach another person the truth, that one can only help him to find it in himself." misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is the most-quoted thing Galileo never said, and it is not really a fake so much as a category error: a nineteenth-century historian’s summary of what a man believed, promoted into what the man wrote.

items.why: It appears in none of his works, and Wikiquote — which lists his quotations work by work, plus an Attributed and a Misattributed section — does not carry it in any of them ↗. The only place it shows up on that page is the caption under his portrait, uncited.

items.scope: The actual source of the English wording
items.why: Read from the scan ↗: “His fundamental maxim, that one cannot teach another person the truth, that one can only help him to find it in himself…” Quinet is characterising Galileo’s method for readers of a polemic against the Church — he supplies no source, and the sentence has never been in quotation marks until other people put it there.

Not a claim we are making for Quinet — he makes it himself, three lines earlier, when he wonders what was the secret demon of “this Socrates of the modern world” ↗. The doctrine that a teacher can only deliver what the pupil already has is Socratic midwifery, and Quinet lent it to Galileo as a compliment.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is real, the book is real, the page is p. 62 — and the man in it is Edgar Quinet, writing about Galileo in 1845 ↗, not Galileo writing about teaching.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Quinet took his Paris chair in 1842 and promptly stopped teaching his own subject ↗, turning the lectern into a weapon against the Jesuits and papal authority alongside his friend Michelet. Galileo is the hero of that argument, and the point of the chapter this sentence sits in is that the Church did not merely punish a man, it truncated a philosophy — that the trial forced Galileo to publish the mathematics and bury the thinking.

So the “fundamental maxim” is doing a job. Quinet needs Galileo to have had a method that was about drawing truth out of people rather than handing it down, because that is the exact opposite of the institution he is attacking. The sentence is an argument in the shape of a quotation, which is why it detached so cleanly and why it now hangs in classrooms.
detailsBody: What Galileo did leave in writing is not far off in spirit, which is part of why the misattribution sticks. The Dialogue’s Salviati tells Simplicio ↗ that in the natural sciences “a thousand Demostheneses and a thousand Aristotles would be left in the lurch by every mediocre wit who happened to hit upon the truth for himself” — which is an argument about authority, and about the pupil arriving at truth unaided. Quinet had read all of that. He then wrote his own sentence for it, and the quotation books have been handing his sentence back to Galileo ever since.

Two things we could not settle, and would rather say so than paper over. We could not read the French original of Quinet’s book, so we cannot show what he wrote before an unnamed translator turned it into this English; the 1845 New York volume names C. Edwards Lester only as editor ↗. And we could not confirm the intermediate stage — the point at which somebody first put the sentence between quotation marks and Galileo’s name under it. Wikiquote’s talk page ↗ shows a trail being followed backwards; ours ends at p. 62.

sourcesVerified.claim: Page 62 of Edgar Quinet's Ultramontanism; or, The Roman Church and Modern Society (New York: Gates & Stedman, 1845) reads "His fundamental maxim, that one cannot teach another person the truth, that one can only help him to find it in himself, which is the foundation of his method, is in itself a whole philosophy," with no quotation marks and no citation, and two sentences earlier calls Galileo "this Socrates of the modern world." Confirmed by reading the page image (page number 62, running head HIS PHILOSOPHY) and the OCR text.

The Internet Archive holds the complete 1845 scan, whose title page reads "Ultramontanism; or, The Roman Church and Modern Society. Translated from the French of Prof. E. Quinet, of the College of France. Edited by C. Edwards Lester," with the imprint "New York: Gates & Stedman, 114 William Street. 1845."

English Wikiquote's Galileo Galilei page does not list "You cannot teach a man anything; you can only help him to find it within himself" in any sourced section, nor under Attributed, nor under Misattributed; the sentence appears on the page only as an uncited image caption. The Dialogue section does carry Salviati's "a thousand Demostheneses and a thousand Aristotles would be left in the lurch by every mediocre wit who happened to hit upon the truth for himself," cited to p. 61.

The talk page for Wikiquote's Galileo Galilei article contains a section "Cannot teach quote attribution date" in which a contributor traces the quote to E. Quinet, The Roman Church and Modern Society, ed. and trans. C. Edwards Lester (New York, 1845), p. 62, giving the wording as "One cannot teach another person the truth, ... one can only help him to find it in himself."

Wikipedia gives Edgar Quinet's dates as 17 February 1803 to 27 March 1875, describes him as a French writer, historian and politician, states his Parisian professorship began in 1842 with the chair of Southern Literature, and that in conjunction with Michelet he engaged in polemic with the Jesuits and with Ultramontanism, with two books bearing exactly those titles appearing in 1843 and 1844.
Wikipedia gives Galileo Galilei's dates as 15 February 1564 to 8 January 1642.
